name: CyberHeaven
description: Free, community-driven cybersecurity learning. Practical guides on OSINT, digital forensics, malware analysis, SOC careers and Linux, written and kept alive by volunteers.
tagline: Free, community-driven cybersecurity learning. Practical guides for every aspiring defender, written and kept alive by volunteers.

tools.title: Alert triage
tools.description: Work a SOC shift: read eight alerts, close the benign ones and escalate the real threats. New alerts every shift.

tools.title: Log hunt
tools.description: Filter a real-looking server log, pin the evidence and work out how the attacker got in. Two cases.
tools.specimen: 03:14:07 sshd: Accepted password for deploy from 203.0.113.45

tools.title: Shell quest
tools.description: Review a copy of a server in a real-feeling Linux terminal. Use ls, cat, grep and find to collect five flags. A new server every game.

tools.title: Decode the layers
tools.description: Peel Base64, hex, URL, ROT13 and XOR layers off suspicious strings, like analysts do in CyberChef. Endless random mode.

tools.title: Real or fake link?
tools.description: Read addresses the way a browser does and spot the lookalike links hiding in emails and texts. New links every round.

tools.title: Write the rule
tools.description: Write a YARA-style detection rule that catches every malware sample and none of the clean files. Scored live as you type.

tools.title: Classify the infection
tools.description: Read what defenders observed on an infected machine, name the type of malware and learn how to respond.
tools.specimen: IR-4821: every file now ends in .locked

tools.title: Spot the phish
tools.description: An inbox of eight messages, shuffled every time. Report the phishing, keep the real ones.

tools.title: Permissions lab
tools.description: Set Linux file permissions with least privilege. Watch ls -l, octal and chmod change live. New tasks every run.

tools.title: Hash and salt
tools.description: See how websites should store passwords: a live SHA-256 hash, why salting matters and how strong a password really is.

tools.title: Fix the query
tools.description: Review code that builds SQL from user input, pick the fix a security reviewer would approve and watch the tests run.

tools.title: Find your path
tools.description: A personal quiz for beginners: every question adapts to your last answer. Get your path, why it fits you and your first three steps.

tools.title: Glossary
tools.description: Plain-English definitions of the cybersecurity terms you’ll run into, from APT to zero trust. Searchable and filterable.

about.statement: Quality cybersecurity learning, free for everyone and powered by the people who use it
about.bio: For eight years CyberHeaven has published practical guides for cybersecurity aspirants. Funding constraints mean we are scaling back and cutting operational costs, so CyberHeaven is now a community-driven, volunteer-contributed project. It isn’t going anywhere: we remain 100% committed to quality content, resources and learning opportunities for everyone.

principles.title: Quality content, always
principles.description: Practical, accurate guides you can actually learn from. Going volunteer-led doesn’t lower the bar.
principles.alt: Blurred charcoal and cream abstract streaks

principles.title: Free for everyone
principles.description: No pricing, no paid courses, no paywalled paths. Everything CyberHeaven publishes is free to read and use.

principles.title: Community-driven
principles.description: Learners shape what comes next. The Discord is led by a community lead responsible for its reforms and restructuring.

principles.title: Volunteer-powered
principles.description: Community contributions keep CyberHeaven active, fresh and valuable. Anyone can write, review or help out.

faq.a: Yes. There is no pricing, no paid courses and no paid learning paths. Every article, lab and tool on CyberHeaven is free for everyone. Our resources page also recommends some outside courses, a few of them paid; we’re not affiliated with any of them.
Volunteers. CyberHeaven is now a community-driven, volunteer-contributed project, and the Discord is led by a community lead responsible for its reforms and restructuring.

faq.q: How can I contribute an article?
faq.a: Share your idea in the Discord or email cyberheavenhq@proton.me with a short outline of the topic. Community contributions are what keep CyberHeaven active and fresh.

faq.q: How do I join the community?
faq.a: Join the CyberHeaven Discord. It’s the place to ask questions, share what you’re learning and meet other cybersecurity aspirants.
Practical, beginner-friendly guides on OSINT, digital forensics and incident response, malware analysis, SOC careers and Linux, with more to come as volunteers contribute.
